knowledge_point.title: Determining the Intercepts of a Normal Line

question.:question/problem: Find where the normal line to the curve $f(x)=2{x}^{2}+x$ at the point $(1,3)$ intersects the $x$-axis.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Taking the derivative, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x)=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{2}+x)=4x+1.\end{aligned}
$$

So the slope of the tangent line is

$$
m={f}^{′}(1)=4(1)+1=5,
$$

and therefore the slope of the normal line is

$$
{m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{5}.
$$

Finally, the equation of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-3 & =-\frac{1}{5}(x-1) \\ y & =-\frac{1}{5}x+\frac{1}{5}+3 \\ y & =-\frac{1}{5}x+\frac{16}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, we find the point of intersection with the $x$-axis by setting $y=0$ and solving the resulting equation. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{5}x+\frac{16}{5} & =0 \\ x & =16.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the normal line intersects the $x$-axis at $(16,0).$

knowledge_point.title: Determining the Intercepts of a Normal Line

question.:question/problem: Find where the normal line to the curve $f(x)=2\sqrt{x}$ at the point $(1,2)$ intersects the $y$-axis.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Taking the derivative, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2\sqrt{x}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{1/2}) \\  & ={x}^{-1/2} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}.\end{aligned}
$$

So the slope of the tangent line is

$$
m={f}^{′}(1)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1}}=1,
$$

and therefore the slope of the normal line is

$$
{m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}=-1.
$$

Finally, the equation of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-2 & =-1(x-1) \\ y & =-x+1+2 \\ y & =-x+3.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, we find the point of intersection with the $y$-axis by setting $x=0$ and solving the resulting equation. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-0+3 \\ y & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the normal line intersects the $y$-axis at  $(0,3).$

question.:question/problem: Find where the normal line to the curve $y={x}^{2}$ at the point $(3,9)$ intersects the $x$-axis.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Taking the derivative, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{'}(x)=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2})=2x.\end{aligned}
$$

So the slope of the tangent line is

$$
m={f}^{'}(3)=2(3)=6,
$$

and therefore the slope of the normal line is

$$
{m}^{'}=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{6}.
$$

Finally, the equation of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-9 & =-\frac{1}{6}(x-3) \\ y & =-\frac{1}{6}x+\frac{1}{2}+9 \\ y & =-\frac{1}{6}x+\frac{19}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, we find the point of intersection with the $x$-axis by setting $y=0$ and solving the resulting equation. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{6}x+\frac{19}{2} & =0 \\ \frac{19}{2} & =\frac{1}{6}x \\ x & =57.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the normal line intersects the $x$-axis at $(57,0).$

question.:question/problem: Find where the normal line to the curve $f(x)=3\sqrt[3]{{x}^{2}}$ at the point $(8,12)$ intersects the $y$-axis.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Taking the derivative, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(3\sqrt[3]{{x}^{2}}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(3{x}^{2/3}) \\  & =2{x}^{-1/3} \\  & =\frac{2}{\sqrt[3]{x}}.\end{aligned}
$$

So the slope of the tangent line is

$$
m={f}^{′}(8)=\frac{2}{\sqrt[3]{8}}=1,
$$

and therefore the slope of the normal line is

$$
{m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}=-1.
$$

Finally, the equation of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-12 & =-(x-8) \\ y & =-x+8+12 \\ y & =20-x.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, we find the point of intersection with the $y$-axis by setting $x=0$ and solving the resulting equation. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =20-0 \\ y & =20.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the normal line intersects the $y$-axis at  $(0,20).$

question.:question/problem: Find where the normal line to the curve $f(x)=2\sqrt{{x}^{3}}$ at the point $(1,2)$ intersects the $x$-axis.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Taking the derivative, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2\sqrt{{x}^{3}}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{3/2}) \\  & =3{x}^{1/2} \\  & =3\sqrt{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

So the slope of the tangent line is

$$
m={f}^{′}(1)=3\sqrt{1}=3,
$$

and therefore the slope of the normal line is

$$
{m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{3}.
$$

Finally, the equation of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-2 & =-\frac{1}{3}(x-1) \\ y & =-\frac{1}{3}x+\frac{1}{3}+2 \\ y & =-\frac{1}{3}x+\frac{7}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, we find the point of intersection with the $x$-axis by setting $y=0$ and solving the resulting equation. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{3}x+\frac{7}{3} & =0 \\ x & =7.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the normal line intersects the $x$-axis at  $(7,0).$

question.:question/problem: Find where the normal line to the curve $f(x)=10 x^{2} + 5 x$ at the point $(1,15)$ intersects the $x$-axis.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Taking the derivative, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f'(x)=\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(10 x^{2} + 5 x)=20 x + 5.\end{aligned}
$$

So the slope of the tangent line is

$$
m=f'(1)=25=25,
$$

and therefore the slope of the normal line is

$$
m'=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{(25)}=- \frac{1}{25}.
$$

Finally, the equation of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-(15)&=- \frac{1}{25}(x-(1))\\y&=- \frac{1}{25}x-\left(- \frac{1}{25}\right)+(15)\\y&=- \frac{1}{25}x+\frac{376}{25}.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, we find the point of intersection with the $x$-axis by setting $y=0$ and solving the resulting equation. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}- \frac{1}{25}x+\frac{376}{25}&=0\\x&=376.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the normal line intersects the $x$-axis at $(376,0).$

question.:question/problem: Find where the normal line to the curve $y={x}^{3}$ at the point $(2,8)$ intersects the $x$-axis.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Taking the derivative, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) &=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{3})=3{x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

So the slope of the tangent line is

$$
m={f}^{′}(2)=3(2)^{2}=12,
$$

and therefore the slope of the normal line is

$$
{m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{12}.
$$

Finally, the equation of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-8 & =-\frac{1}{12}(x-(2)) \\ y & =-\frac{1}{12}x+\frac{1}{6}+8 \\ y & =-\frac{1}{12}x+\frac{49}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, we find the point of intersection with the $x$-axis by setting $y=0$ and solving the resulting equation. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{12}x+\frac{49}{6} & =0 \\ \frac{1}{12}x & =\frac{49}{6} \\ x & =98\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the normal line intersects the $x$-axis at $(98,0).$

knowledge_point.title: Determining the Intercepts of a Normal Line

question.:question/problem: Find where the normal line to the curve $y=x^2$ at the point $(1,1)$ intersects the $x$-axis.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Differentiating gives

$$
f'(x)=2x,\qquad f'(1)=2.
$$

The tangent slope is $2$, so the normal slope is its negative reciprocal:

$$
m_n=-\frac{1}{2}.
$$

The diagram shows the curve, its solid tangent, and its dashed normal at $(1,1)$.

![The parabola y equals x squared with its tangent and perpendicular normal at (1,1).](images/31/31ba09ff14e5bd485794f283c5d6a5b087b6c21fdb9242af01b75ec8e8744e0d.png)

Using point-slope form, the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}
y-1&=-\frac{1}{2}(x-1)\\
y&=-\frac{1}{2}x+\frac{3}{2}.
\end{aligned}
$$

At the $x$-axis, $y=0$. Therefore,

$$
0=-\frac{1}{2}x+\frac{3}{2},\qquad x=3.
$$

The intersection is $(3,0)$.
